notes.definition: The brain controls complex behaviour. It is made of billions of interconnected neurones and has different regions that carry out different functions.
explanation: The brain is part of the central nervous system. It contains billions of neurones, each connected to many others, so it can process huge amounts of information at once. This is what allows it to control complex behaviour such as speech, learning and decision making. Different regions of the brain specialise in different functions, although they also work together.

You need to know three regions. The cerebral cortex is the large, folded outer layer at the top of the brain. It is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language. The cerebellum is at the back, below the cerebral cortex. It is responsible for the coordination of muscular activity, which includes balance and smooth, accurate movement.

The medulla is at the base of the brain, where it joins the spinal cord. It controls unconscious activities such as the heartbeat and breathing. Damage to the medulla can therefore be life-threatening, because these vital processes may stop working properly.

Neuroscientists have mapped regions of the brain to particular functions in three main ways. They study patients with brain damage: if damage to one area causes a particular ability to be lost, that area is probably involved in that ability. They electrically stimulate different parts of the brain with electrodes and record what happens, such as a muscle moving or a memory being recalled. They use MRI scanning, which produces detailed images of the brain and can show which areas become active while a person carries out a task, without needing surgery.

The brain is complex and delicate, which makes investigating and treating brain disorders very difficult. Surgery may damage healthy tissue that controls other functions, there is a risk of infection or bleeding, and damaged neurones rarely repair themselves. Drugs may affect other parts of the brain. Before any procedure on the brain or nervous system, doctors weigh the benefits (for example removing a tumour or reducing tremors) against these risks.
keyFacts: It is made of billions of interconnected neurones.
Different regions carry out different functions.
Cerebral cortex: consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.
Cerebellum: coordination of muscular activity (including balance).
Medulla: unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
Brain regions are mapped by studying brain damage, electrical stimulation and MRI scanning.
The brain is complex and delicate, so investigating and treating disorders is difficult.
Procedures on the brain have benefits and risks that must be evaluated.

keyTerms.definition: The folded outer layer of the brain, responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.
The region at the back of the brain that coordinates muscular activity.
The region at the base of the brain, joining the spinal cord, that controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
Applying a small electric current to an area of the brain with an electrode to see what response it causes.
Magnetic resonance imaging: a non-invasive technique that produces detailed images of the brain and can show which areas are active.
A scientist who studies the brain and nervous system.

workedExamples.title: Linking symptoms to a brain region
workedExamples.question: After a head injury, a patient can think and speak normally, but their movements are clumsy and they find it hard to keep their balance. Suggest which region of the brain is damaged and explain your answer.
steps: List the symptoms: movement and balance are affected.
Recall that the cerebellum coordinates muscular activity.
Check the other regions: speech and thinking (cerebral cortex) are normal, and there is no mention of breathing or heartbeat problems (medulla).
workedExamples.answer: The cerebellum, because it coordinates muscular activity, and the patient's thinking and language (cerebral cortex) are unaffected.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a brain procedure
workedExamples.question: Deep brain stimulation involves placing electrodes in the brain to reduce tremors in Parkinson's disease. Evaluate this procedure.
steps: Give benefits: tremors may be greatly reduced, improving quality of life; the stimulation can be adjusted or switched off.
Give risks: surgery on the brain may damage healthy tissue; risk of infection or bleeding; side effects such as changes in mood or speech; it does not cure the disease.
workedExamples.answer: It can greatly improve quality of life when drugs no longer work, but because the brain is delicate there are serious risks, so it is only used when the benefits are likely to outweigh the risks.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the cerebellum is responsible for thinking and memory.
misconceptions.right: In fact the cerebral cortex is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language. The cerebellum coordinates muscular activity.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the medulla controls conscious actions like walking.
misconceptions.right: In fact the medulla controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think MRI scanning involves surgery or radiation that damages the brain.
misconceptions.right: In fact MRI is non-invasive and uses magnetic fields and radio waves, so no surgery is needed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think each region works completely on its own.
misconceptions.right: In fact regions are specialised, but they are connected by billions of neurones and work together.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think damaged brain tissue can easily be repaired or replaced.
misconceptions.right: In fact neurones rarely regenerate, which is one reason brain damage and disease are difficult to treat.

realWorld: In 1848 Phineas Gage survived an iron rod passing through the front of his brain; his change in personality gave early evidence that particular regions control particular behaviours.

During epilepsy surgery, the neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield electrically stimulated the cortex of awake patients and recorded the movements, sensations and memories produced, building some of the first brain maps.
Functional MRI scans are used before surgery to locate areas controlling speech and movement so surgeons can avoid them.
Deep brain stimulation is used to reduce tremors in some people with Parkinson's disease.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology (8461) only, not in Combined Science Trilogy.
Identify the cerebral cortex, cerebellum and medulla and describe their functions.
Explain how brain regions are mapped using brain damage studies, electrical stimulation and MRI scanning.
Evaluate the benefits and risks of procedures carried out on the brain and nervous system.
examTips: Learn each region with its AQA function word for word: cortex (consciousness, intelligence, memory, language), cerebellum (coordination of muscular activity), medulla (unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing).
Practise labelling a diagram: the cerebellum is the small ridged structure at the back and bottom; the medulla is the stalk joining the spinal cord.
When asked to "explain how" a mapping method works, describe what is done AND how this links a region to a function.
In "evaluate" questions give benefits and risks, then finish with a justified conclusion.
Use the phrase "complex and delicate" when explaining why brain disorders are hard to treat.
summary: The brain controls complex behaviour and is made of billions of interconnected neurones.
Cerebral cortex: consciousness, intelligence, memory, language.
Medulla: unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
Regions are mapped using brain damage studies, electrical stimulation and MRI.
Brain treatments are difficult and risky because the brain is complex and delicate.

flashcards.front: What is the brain made of?
flashcards.back: Billions of interconnected neurones, organised into regions with different functions.
Unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
At the back of the brain, below the cerebral cortex.
At the base of the brain, where it joins the spinal cord.

flashcards.front: How do brain damage studies map the brain?
flashcards.back: If damage to one area causes loss of a function, that area is linked to that function.

flashcards.front: How does electrical stimulation map the brain?
flashcards.back: An electrode applies a small current to an area and the response (movement, sensation, memory) is recorded.

flashcards.front: How does MRI help map the brain?
flashcards.back: It produces detailed images and shows which areas are active during a task, without surgery.

flashcards.front: Why are brain disorders hard to treat?
flashcards.back: The brain is complex and delicate, so treatment can damage healthy tissue, and neurones rarely repair.

flashcards.front: Give two risks of brain surgery.
flashcards.back: Damage to healthy brain tissue (affecting other functions); infection or bleeding.

questions.question: Which region of the brain is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language?
markScheme: 1 mark: cerebral cortex
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is the large, folded outer layer responsible for these higher functions. The spinal cord is not part of the brain.

questions.question: Which region of the brain coordinates muscular activity?
markScheme: 1 mark: cerebellum
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscular activity and balance. The pituitary is a gland, not a region you need to know for this function.

questions.question: Which region of the brain controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing?
markScheme: 1 mark: medulla
questions.explanation: The medulla, at the base of the brain, controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing.

questions.question: What is the brain made of?
options: A few large neurones that are not connected
markScheme: 1 mark: billions of interconnected neurones
questions.explanation: The brain contains billions of neurones linked together, which allows it to control complex behaviour.

questions.question: A patient has a damaged cerebellum. Which problem are they most likely to have?
options: Difficulty with balance and coordinating movements
markScheme: 1 mark: difficulty with balance and coordinating movements
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscular activity. Memory is linked to the cerebral cortex and breathing to the medulla.

questions.question: Which technique allows scientists to see which areas of the brain are active during a task without surgery?
options: Removing small samples of brain tissue
markScheme: 1 mark: MRI scanning
questions.explanation: MRI scanning is non-invasive and can show active areas while a person does a task. Electrical stimulation requires electrodes to be placed on or in the brain.

questions.question: An accident damages a patient's medulla. Which effect is most likely?
options: Loss of their ability to read
Problems with their heart rate and breathing
markScheme: 1 mark: problems with heart rate and breathing
questions.explanation: The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heartbeat and breathing, so damage can affect these vital functions.

questions.question: During surgery, a small electric current is applied to one area of a conscious patient's cerebral cortex. The patient's left hand twitches. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: This area controls all movements of the body
This area is involved in controlling movement of the left hand
Electrical current always causes movement wherever it is applied
markScheme: 1 mark: this area is involved in controlling movement of the left hand
questions.explanation: Stimulating one area produced one specific response, so that area is linked to that function. It does not show the area controls all movement, and stimulating other areas causes different responses (or none), such as memories or sensations.

questions.question: Why can studying patients with brain damage give limited evidence about the function of a single brain region?
options: Patients with brain damage cannot be studied ethically at all
Damage often affects more than one region, and scientists cannot control where or how much damage occurs
The brain is made of only one type of tissue
markScheme: 1 mark: damage often affects several regions and cannot be controlled
questions.explanation: In natural damage (for example strokes or injuries) the size and position of the damage vary and often cover several regions, so it is hard to link a lost function to one exact area.

questions.question: A person who has drunk a lot of alcohol walks unsteadily and has poor coordination. Which brain region is this most likely to show has been affected?
markScheme: 1 mark: cerebellum
questions.explanation: Unsteady walking and poor coordination suggest the cerebellum, which coordinates muscular activity, is not working normally.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why it is difficult to treat brain disorders?
options: The brain has only a few neurones, so any damage is serious
Brain cells divide very quickly, so tumours always return
The brain is not connected to the rest of the nervous system
The brain is complex and delicate, so treatment may damage healthy tissue and affect other functions
markScheme: 1 mark: complex and delicate, so treatment risks damaging healthy tissue
questions.explanation: The brain has billions of interconnected neurones and is easily damaged, so surgery or drugs can harm areas controlling other functions.

questions.question: Scientists compare the location of a patient's brain damage with the abilities the patient has lost. Which method of mapping the brain is this?
markScheme: 1 mark: studying patients with brain damage
questions.explanation: Linking the area of damage to the lost function is the brain damage method.

questions.question: Which region of the brain is directly connected to the spinal cord?
markScheme: 1 mark: medulla
questions.explanation: The medulla is at the base of the brain and joins the spinal cord.

questions.question: State the function of the medulla.
markScheme: 1 mark: controls unconscious activities
1 mark: such as heartbeat / breathing
questions.explanation: The medulla controls unconscious activities, for example heartbeat and breathing.

questions.question: Give two functions of the cerebral cortex.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: consciousness; intelligence; memory; language
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.

questions.question: Describe how studying patients with brain damage has helped scientists to map the brain.
markScheme: 1 mark: identify which area of the brain is damaged (for example after death or with a scan)
1 mark: link it to the ability / function the patient has lost
questions.explanation: If a patient loses a particular ability and the damage is in a particular area, that area is probably involved in that ability.

questions.question: Describe how electrical stimulation is used to find out the function of a region of the brain.
markScheme: 1 mark: an electrode is used to pass a small electric current into / onto an area of the brain
1 mark: the response (for example a movement, sensation or memory) is observed and linked to that area
questions.explanation: Stimulating one area at a time and recording the result builds up a map of what each area does.

questions.question: Explain how MRI scanning can be used to identify which parts of the brain are involved in language.
markScheme: 1 mark: person is scanned while carrying out a language task (for example speaking or reading)
1 mark: areas that are active / have increased activity show up on the image, so they are linked to language
questions.explanation: MRI produces detailed images and can show which areas are most active during a task, linking those areas to the function.

questions.question: Suggest three risks of carrying out surgery on the brain.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 3: damage to healthy brain tissue; loss of other functions such as memory, speech or movement; infection; bleeding; damage may be permanent as neurones rarely repair; the procedure may not cure the problem
questions.explanation: Because the brain is complex and delicate, surgery can damage areas other than the target, and the damage may be permanent.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using MRI scanning rather than electrical stimulation to study the brain.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage: non-invasive / no surgery needed / can be used on healthy volunteers
1 mark: disadvantage: expensive / person must lie still in an enclosed scanner / cannot be used with some metal implants
questions.explanation: MRI avoids opening the skull, but scanners are expensive and some people cannot be scanned.

questions.question: Explain why the brain is able to control complex behaviour.
markScheme: 1 mark: made of billions of interconnected neurones (so huge amounts of information can be processed)
1 mark: different regions carry out different / specialised functions and work together
questions.explanation: Complex behaviour needs lots of information to be processed and coordinated at once, which is possible because of the number and connections of neurones and the specialisation of regions.

questions.question: After a stroke, a patient can understand speech but cannot form words to speak. Suggest which region of the brain was damaged and what this tells scientists about brain function.
markScheme: 1 mark: (part of) the cerebral cortex
1 mark: a specific part of the brain controls a specific function / different parts of language are controlled by different areas
questions.explanation: Language is a function of the cerebral cortex. Losing speech but not understanding shows that different areas are responsible for different parts of language, which is evidence that brain regions are specialised.

questions.question: Explain why damage to the medulla is often life-threatening.
markScheme: 1 mark: the medulla controls heartbeat / breathing
1 mark: these are vital processes, so if they stop or become irregular the person may die
questions.explanation: The medulla controls unconscious but vital activities. Without them, cells would not get oxygen.

questions.question: Suggest two reasons why it is difficult for scientists to investigate how the human brain works.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: the brain is very complex (billions of interconnected neurones); it is delicate / easily damaged; it is unethical to damage or experiment on healthy brains; many methods are invasive; regions work together so it is hard to isolate one function
questions.explanation: The complexity and delicacy of the brain, together with ethical limits, make experiments difficult.

questions.question: Name the three regions of the brain that you should be able to identify on a diagram of the brain.
markScheme: 1 mark: cerebral cortex
1 mark: cerebellum
1 mark: medulla
questions.explanation: The three regions to identify are the cerebral cortex, cerebellum and medulla.

questions.question: Describe three methods that neuroscientists have used to map the regions of the brain to particular functions.
markScheme: Indicative content: studying patients with brain damage: identify the area damaged and link to the function lost; electrical stimulation: electrode passes a small current into an area, observe the movement, sensation or memory produced; MRI scanning: produces detailed images; scan during a task shows which areas are active; MRI is non-invasive.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all three methods described with clear explanation of how each links a region to a function.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or more methods named or described simply, with little link to function.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: For each method, say what is done and how it links a particular region to a particular function.

questions.question: A patient has a tumour in the cerebral cortex. Doctors are considering surgery to remove it. Evaluate the use of surgery to treat this patient.
markScheme: Indicative content: benefits: removing the tumour may stop it growing and pressing on the brain; may prolong life or cure; may relieve symptoms such as headaches or seizures; MRI scans can locate the tumour precisely and map nearby areas so surgeons avoid them. Risks: the brain is complex and delicate; surgery may damage healthy tissue in the cerebral cortex; this could affect consciousness, intelligence, memory or language; neurones rarely repair so damage may be permanent; infection or bleeding; it may not be possible to remove all of the tumour; anaesthetic risks. Conclusion: surgery is justified if the benefits (for example survival) outweigh the risks, which depends on the size and position of the tumour and the patient's wishes.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a balanced evaluation with detailed benefits and risks linked to the functions of the cerebral cortex, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some benefits and risks given, with some links to brain function; conclusion may be missing or not justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of a benefit or a risk.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Evaluate means weighing both sides and reaching a conclusion. The best answers link risks to what the cerebral cortex does and explain how scans can reduce the risk.
